ety.text: Borrowed from French banal + -ный (-nyj). Further from Latin bannālis, from Latin bannus (whence also English abandon). Further from Proto-Germanic *bannaną (whence also English ban). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to speak”).

Borrowed in the second half of 18th century (first attested in 1785, form барказ (barkaz) in 1762) from Dutch barkas (“a large or the largest row-boat on a ship”) (att. since 1718), Swedish barkasse (since 1765) or possibly another Western European language, from some Romance language. Compare Italian barcaccia. Ultimately from Latin barca. Doublet of баржа́ (baržá) and ба́рка (bárka).

tpl.gloss: a large or the largest row-boat on a ship

x: Вико́нт был милови́дный, с мя́гкими черта́ми и приёмами, молодо́й челове́к, очеви́дно счита́вший себя́ знамени́тостью, но, по благовоспи́танности, скро́мно предоставля́вший по́льзоваться собо́й тому́ о́бществу, в кото́ром он находи́лся.
Молоды́е вы́пили по бока́лу, переоде́лись и пое́хали на вокза́л.

ety.text: Borrowed from French bocal, from Italian boccale.

x: Е́сли челове́к не поспи́т тро́е су́ток, он стано́вится бо́лен и пло́хо по́мнит, а они́ не спят уже́ неде́лю, и они́ все сумасше́дшие.

s.g: patient (someone receiving treatment for an illness)

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic Вадимъ (Vadimŭ), diminutive of Вадимиръ (Vadimirŭ); compare вадить (vaditʹ, “to argue; to tame”) (see Proto-Slavic *vaditi).

s.g: a female given name from Ancient Greek, equivalent to English Veronica

ety.text: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Βερονίκη, Βερενίκη (Beroníkē, Bereníkē), from φέρω (phérō) + νῑ́κη (nī́kē), as if bringer of victory.

s.g: to appeal (to God for mercy, justice, vengeance, etc.)
to cry out, to yell, to scream
to lament, to wail for the dead

ety.text: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic въпити (vŭpiti) with levelling of the present stem. Ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *vъpìti.
Clipped compound of госуда́рственный о́рган (gosudárstvennyj órgan, “state agency”).

s.g: the civil script, a modernized version of the Cyrillic script, introduced by Peter I of Russia in 1708

x: Скро́мная черёмуха перестаёт благоуха́ть. И го́рький за́пах ряби́ны стыди́тся пе́ред пьяня́щим за́пахом сире́ни. Но — сире́нь. Тебя́ ждёт больша́я неприя́тность — расцветёт жасми́н и свои́м за́пахом земляни́ки и огурца́ заглуши́т твой ца́рственный за́пах.

s.g: jasmine flowers (esp. used for tea, etc.)
initialism of знание — сила (znanije — sila, “knowledge is power”)
The Green Elephant, a 1999 Russian horror film set in an abusive Soviet army base used as a source for many humorous Internet memes.

ety.text: Initialism of Зелёный сло́ник (Zeljónyj slónik, “green elephant calf”). The movie's title was from a song sang by one of the characters in the film.
Borrowed from French caïque. Doublet of каю́к (kajúk).
Inherited from Old East Slavic кънѧжити (kŭnęžiti), equivalent to княг- (knjag-) + -ить (-itʹ), based on the original stem княг- (knjag-) of князь (knjazʹ); compare feminine княги́ня (knjagínja).

Inherited from Old East Slavic крꙑ (kry), from Proto-Slavic *kry, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *krū́ˀs, from Proto-Indo-European *krewh₂- (“blood of a wound”). Cognate with Latin cruor (“blood(shed)”), Lithuanian kraujas, Welsh crau, English raw.

s.g: Kursk (a city, the administrative center of Kursk Oblast, Russia)

ety.text: By surface analysis, Кур (Kur, “Kur River”) + -ск (-sk). Possibly related to курья́ (kurʹjá) or ку́рица (kúrica).

s.g: a surname, Leontyev, also written Leontief, Leontiev, etc.; surname of various notable Russians and Soviets
poisoner (person who poisons something or someone)
to dumbfound, to strike dumb, to flabbergast, to bowl out

ety.text: пере- (pere-) + межи́ть (mežítʹ, “to delineate the boundary of”)

x: прилете́ли к нам грачи́, пидора́сы москвичи́

И́стинно, они́ ху́же мух, и́бо му́хи то́лько и́зредка согреша́ют на мое́й голове́, пидара́сы же и́зо дня в день пыта́ются совокупи́ться в са́мом её це́нтре. Му́хи по недомы́слию, пидара́сы же хладнокро́вно и созна́тельно.

s.g: spilling over after spring ice breakup (of water or a river)

ety.text: Inherited from Old East Slavic полъ (polŭ, “open from above, uncovered”), attested in a 14th-c. birchbark letter (No. 59) in "полои води" 'floodwaters.GEN.SG' (cf. Russian половодье (polovodʹje)). Modern meaning attested since 1636. Related to Proto-Slavic *poľe (“field”) and *polnъ (“flat, smooth, plain”), both from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

s.g: to start carrying (unwillingly or something heavy)
to come in handy, to prove useful

ety.text: Borrowed from Old Church Slavonic приобрѣсти (priobrěsti). By surface analysis, при- (pri-) + обрести́ (obrestí).

s.g: to exchange (for), to trade (for), to barter (for), to truck (for)
Hrazdan (a town, the capital of Kotayk Province, Armenia)
to grow flabby, to become soft

ety.text: From French raccourci (“shortcut; foreshortening”). Omitting several steps, from Latin re- + ad- + Latin curtus. Comare typologically вкра́тце (vkrátce). Note natively formed Polish ujęcie (i.e. **уятье).

s.g: Silesian (relating to Silesia, a region spanning parts of Poland, Germany and the Czech Republic)

avaricious, stingy, frugal, mean, parsimonious, miserly

Inherited from Old East Slavic скупъ (skupŭ), from Proto-Slavic *skǫpъ.

x: Локонов чу́вствовал, что он явля́ется ча́стью како́й-то карти́ны. ety.text: трёх- (trjox-) + ли́ния (línija) + -ка (-ka), from три ли́нии (tri línii, “3 lines (in the historical sense of tenths of an inch)”), the rifle's caliber (7.62 mm in metric units).
